The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563 and was the Roman Catholic Church's major ecumenical council convened to address the theological challenges posed by the Protestant Reformation and to reform Catholic doctrine and practice. Meeting in the northern Italian city of Trent over eighteen years in multiple sessions, the council reaffirmed core Catholic doctrines, standardized liturgical practice through the Tridentine Latin Mass, and initiated internal reforms to address corruption and improve clerical education. The council was convened by Pope Paul III initially in response to the spread of Protestantism. It aimed to clarify Catholic doctrine and prevent further schism. The council reaffirmed papal authority against Protestant claims of sola scriptura, scripture alone, asserting the binding authority of both scripture and sacred tradition. Trent affirmed the practice of venerating saints and images, the theological reality of purgatory, and the sacramental nature of marriage and other rituals, all contested by Protestants. The council mandated the standardization of the Latin Mass, called the Tridentine Mass, and required strict observance of liturgical uniformity throughout the Catholic world. It established the Vulgate, Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible, as the official Catholic text and commissioned a corrected edition to counter Protestant Biblical scholarship. The council initiated reforms addressing clerical celibacy, education, discipline, and simony, laying groundwork for the Counter-Reformation.
